1.q: לְמַ֤עַן צִיּוֹן֙ לֹ֣א אֶחֱשֶׁ֔ה וּ⁠לְמַ֥עַן יְרוּשָׁלִַ֖ם לֹ֣א & אֶשְׁק֑וֹט
1.note: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of clauses in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [Because I care about Zion, that is, Jerusalem, I will not stop speaking out on her behalf]

Isaiah is emphasizing a positive meaning by using a negative word, **not**, together with a mild expression that is the opposite of the intended meaning. If it would be helpful in your language, you could emphasize the positive meaning in a strong way. Alternate translation: [I will keep speaking out]

1.q: עַד־יֵצֵ֤א כַ⁠נֹּ֨גַהּ֙ צִדְקָ֔⁠הּ וִ⁠ישׁוּעָתָ֖⁠הּ כְּ⁠לַפִּ֥יד יִבְעָֽר
1.note: Isaiah is speaking of **righteousness** as if it were something that potentially **goes forth** and of **salvation** as if were something that potentially **burns**. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [until its righteousness and salvation become clearly evident]

The point of this comparison is that just as **brightness** shines out for everyone to see when the day dawns, so **its righteousness** will become plainly visible to all the nations. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [its righteousness becomes plainly visible to everyone, as the light of dawn is visible to all]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [its righteous deeds]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a torch** burns brightly and can be seen in the darkness, so **its salvation** will shine out for all to see. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and its salvation shines out brightly for all to see]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and how God saves it]

2.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how you are righteous]

Isaiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and all of the kings will see your glory]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **glory**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how glorious you are]
The word **one** here refers to people in general, not to a specific individual. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and people will call]

The words **you** and **your** are feminine singular because they refer to Zion, personified as a woman. Those words are feminine singular in verses 3–9 and 11–12 for the same reason. So use singular forms in your translation if your language marks that distinction, and use feminine forms if your language marks that distinction.

Isaiah is using **the mouth of Yahweh** to represent Yahweh himself in the act of speaking. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh personally]

3.q: עֲטֶ֥רֶת תִּפְאֶ֖רֶת בְּ⁠יַד יְהוָ֑ה ו⁠צנוף מְלוּכָ֖ה בְּ⁠כַף אֱלֹהָֽיִ⁠ךְ
3.note: Isaiah is speaking of the people of Jerusalem as if they were **a crown of beauty in the hand of Yahweh, and a turban of kingship in the palm of your God**. He means that Yahweh will display them as a glorious sign of his honor. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a glorious sign of Yahweh’s honor, something your God is proud to display]

Isaiah is using the possessive form **your God** to express the relationship of worship between the people and God, rather than ownership. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the God whom you worship]

4.note: The expression **It will no longer be said** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [No one will any longer say of you]

The expression **it will be called** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [people will call you]
The word **Hephzibah** is the name of a woman, meaning “My delight is in her,” which Yahweh gives here as a symbolic new name for Jerusalem. Alternate translation: [“My Delight Is in Her”]

The expression **your land will be married** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh will marry your land]

The word **Beulah** is the name of a woman. It means “married.” If it would be helpful to your readers, you could indicate this in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [Married]

Isaiah is speaking of the land as if it were a woman that would be **married**. He means that the people will again live in the land and care for it, as a husband lives with and cares for his wife. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and your people will again live in your land and care for it]

5.note: Isaiah is not referring to a specific **young man** or **young woman**. He means young men and young women in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [young men marry young women]

Isaiah is speaking of the people who will inhabit Jerusalem as if they were bridegrooms marrying the city. Just as **a young man marries a young woman** and lives with her, so **your sons will marry you** and dwell in you permanently. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a young man settles down permanently with a young woman, your sons will settle down and live in you]

5.q: וּ⁠מְשׂ֤וֹשׂ חָתָן֙ עַל כַּלָּ֔ה יָשִׂ֥ישׂ עָלַ֖יִ⁠ךְ אֱלֹהָֽיִ⁠ךְ
5.note: Isaiah is speaking of God’s joy over his people as if it were the joy that a bridegroom feels for his bride. Just as **a bridegroom** rejoices **over a bride**, so **your God will rejoice over you**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And just as a bridegroom rejoices over his bride, so your God will rejoice over you]

6.note: Isaiah is speaking of the people whom Yahweh has appointed to pray persistently for Jerusalem as if they were **watchmen on your walls**. Just as watchmen keep guard over a city day and night, these intercessors continually remind Yahweh of his promises. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [people to intercede for you continually]

Isaiah is referring to all of time by naming its two extremes, **All of the day** and **all of the night**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [At every hour]

The terms **all of the day and all of the night** and **continually** mean similar things. Isaiah is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [at every moment, without stopping]

Isaiah is emphasizing a positive meaning by using a negative word, **not**, together with a mild expression, **silent**, that is the opposite of the intended meaning. If it would be helpful in your language, you could emphasize the positive meaning in a strong way. Alternate translation: [they will speak out continually]

7.note: Isaiah is using **do not give quiet to him** as a common expression of the culture to mean “do not stop appealing to him.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and do not stop appealing to him]

Here, **a praise in the earth** represents “something that people throughout the earth praise.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [something that people throughout the earth praise]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **praise**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [something that people praise]

8.note: Following the custom of the culture, Yahweh is swearing an oath by stating the first part of a condition (“if”) but not the second part (“then”). If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explicitly state the second part of this condition. Alternate translation: [Yahweh has sworn by his right hand and by the arm of his strength that he will never let the following happen]

Here, **his right hand** and **the arm of his strength** represent “Yahweh’s power.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [by his own mighty power]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **strength**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and by his strong arm]

Isaiah is using **the sons of foreignness** as a common expression of the culture to mean “foreigners.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [people from other nations]

9.q: כִּ֤י מְאַסְפָי⁠ו֙ יֹאכְלֻ֔⁠הוּ וְ⁠הִֽלְל֖וּ אֶת יְהוָ֑ה וּֽ⁠מְקַבְּצָ֥י⁠ו יִשְׁתֻּ֖⁠הוּ בְּ⁠חַצְר֥וֹת קָדְשִֽׁ⁠י
9.note: Isaiah uses the word **For** here to indicate a contrast between what Yahweh said would no longer happen, that enemies would consume the harvest, and what will happen instead, that those who gather the harvest will eat and drink it themselves. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Instead, its collectors will eat it and praise Yahweh, and its gatherers will drink it in the courts of my holiness]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **holiness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in my holy courts]

10.q: עִבְר֤וּ עִבְרוּ֙ בַּ⁠שְּׁעָרִ֔ים פַּנּ֖וּ דֶּ֣רֶךְ הָ⁠עָ֑ם סֹ֣לּוּ סֹ֤לּוּ הַֽ⁠מְסִלָּה֙ סַקְּל֣וּ מֵ⁠אֶ֔בֶן הָרִ֥ימוּ נֵ֖ס עַל־הָ⁠עַמִּֽים
10.note: The implied “you” in the imperatives in this verse is plural. (As in 57:14, the addressees are not named, but the context suggests that they are the other nations that have kept the Israelites captive and must now free and return them.) The implied “you” in the imperative “Say” in the next verse is similarly plural. So use plural forms in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

11.note: Isaiah is using **the end of the earth** to represent the entire earth, that is, even its most distant places. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to the most distant places on earth]

11.q: אִמְרוּ֙ לְ⁠בַת־צִיּ֔וֹן הִנֵּ֥ה יִשְׁעֵ֖⁠ךְ בָּ֑א הִנֵּ֤ה שְׂכָר⁠וֹ֙ אִתּ֔⁠וֹ וּ⁠פְעֻלָּת֖⁠וֹ לְ⁠פָנָֽי⁠ו
11.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Tell the daughter of Zion that behold, her salvation is coming! Tell her that behold, his wage is with him, and his reward is to his face]

Isaiah is using **the daughter of Zion** as a common expression of the culture to mean “the people of Jerusalem.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to the people of Jerusalem]

Here, **your salvation** represents “the one who saves you.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the one who rescues you is coming]

Yahweh is using the term **Behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Look, your salvation is coming! Look, his wage is with him]

Here, **his wage** and **his reward** represent “the people he has rescued, whom he brings with him.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the people he has rescued are with him, and those he has redeemed go before him]

12.note: The expression **it will be called** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [they will refer as]
